Alexander I. A ruler whose progressive idealism curdled into rigid conservatism, shaped by the trauma of empire. He ascended to the throne in 1801 after his father Paul I's assassination, possibly aware of the conspiracy that made him tsar. Though initially an enlightened monarch influenced by Enlightenment thought, he would end his reign as the architect of European reaction.

Early in his rule, Alexander appointed progressive advisors, particularly Mikhail Speransky. Together they implemented sweeping administrative reforms, new legal codes, and expanded education. He even flirted with constitutionalism, granting Poland and Finland a degree of autonomy as semi-independent kingdoms within the empire. Yet gradually, after 1810, he abandoned these reforms and turned instead toward conservatism and Orthodox mysticism.

The pivotal moment came in 1812 when Napoleon invaded Russia with the Grande Armée. Alexander refused capitulation despite initial military defeats. The Russian strategy was simple but devastating: retreat, burn the land as you go, and let the winter do the work. The Grande Armée was destroyed. Napoleon was forced to retreat from Russian soil.

Alexander pursued him westward, leading the coalition armies into Europe. He was instrumental in forcing Napoleon's abdication in 1814. He returned to Russia as the savior of Europe and the continent's most influential voice in shaping the post-war settlement. At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, he played the leading role in redrawing European boundaries and installing conservative monarchs.

That same year, he founded the Holy Alliance—a loose conservative coalition of European monarchs pledging to uphold Christian principles and monarchical legitimacy. In practice, it became the instrument of reactionary suppression. Using Russian military power, Alexander intervened across Europe to crush revolutions in Spain, Greece, and elsewhere. He became, as historians put it, the gendarme of the old order.

Territorially, he expanded relentlessly. He annexed Georgia in 1801 and acquired other Caucasian territories from the Ottoman and Persian empires. Through the Congress of Vienna, he gained significant Polish territory, making Poland a Russian satellite. He expanded influence in the Mediterranean and Near East at Ottoman expense.

In his later years, increasingly isolated and melancholic, he withdrew from public life, reportedly haunted by the destruction he had witnessed. He shares a father with his predecessor and a darker parallel with his brother Nicholas I, who carried the conservative turn to extremes. He was shaped by Napoleon and by the Congress of Vienna, where he emerged as Europe's leading statesman. His reign marks the moment Russian progressivism caved to the weight of empire.
